lesson.title: Securing Bits: The Basics of Cryptography
lesson.summary: Introduces the four goals of cryptography, confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, and the mechanisms (symmetric/asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures) networks use to achieve them.
lesson.body:
You already know that everything traveling across a network is just a stream of bits, and that's exactly the problem: bits have no built-in protection. Anyone with access to the wire or the airwaves can copy them, flip them, or send fake ones pretending to be you. Cryptography is the set of techniques for taking these vulnerable bits and transforming them so that four specific guarantees can hold: confidentiality (only the intended party can read the content), integrity (nobody tampered with it along the way), authentication (you know who really sent it), and non-repudiation (the sender can't later deny having sent it).

The core trick behind confidentiality is encryption: scrambling data using a secret key so that the output is unreadable without that key. There are two main flavors. Symmetric encryption uses the same key to scramble and unscramble the data. It's fast and efficient, which is why it handles the bulk of actual data transfer, but it has a hard logistical problem: both sides need the identical secret key before they can talk, and getting that key to the other party over an insecure network seems circular. Asymmetric encryption solves this by using a mathematically linked pair of keys ,  a public one that can be shared with anyone, and a private one kept secret. Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key. This lets two strangers establish a shared symmetric key over an open network without ever transmitting that key in the clear: one side encrypts a freshly generated symmetric key using the other's public key, and only the intended recipient's private key can recover it. Because asymmetric math is computationally heavier, real systems use it briefly, just to exchange a symmetric key, then switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual conversation.

Integrity and authentication rely on a different tool: the hash function, which takes an input of any size and produces a fixed-size fingerprint, such that even a one-bit change in the input produces a wildly different fingerprint, and you can't feasibly work backward from the fingerprint to reconstruct the input. If you send a message along with its hash, a receiver can recompute the hash and check it matches ,  catching accidental corruption or deliberate tampering. But a plain hash alone doesn't prove who sent it, since anyone could recompute and attach a fresh hash. Combining a hash with a secret key (so only someone holding that key could have produced the correct hash for that message) gives you a way to confirm both integrity and that the message came from someone who knows the shared secret.

Non-repudiation and stronger authentication come from digital signatures, which flip the asymmetric trick around: the sender encrypts (or more precisely, signs) a hash of the message using their own private key. Anyone can verify the signature using the sender's public key, but only the holder of that private key could have created it ,  so the sender can't credibly claim someone else sent it.

A real-world example that ties all of this together is a TLS connection, the kind your browser sets up for a secure website: asymmetric cryptography negotiates a shared symmetric key, symmetric encryption then protects the actual data flowing back and forth, and keyed hashing checks that none of it was altered in transit.
